blocks.text: Adapter loading is the practice of keeping a fine-tuned LoRA adapter, covered in earlier modules, separate from its base model at deployment time, loading it dynamically at runtime rather than merging it permanently into the model weights.

This topic covers how runtime adapter loading works, why it enables serving multiple task-specific behaviors from one shared base model, and the latency tradeoffs that come with swapping adapters dynamically.
1. What Adapter Loading Means

blocks.alt: A deployed base model loads an adapter at runtime, producing task specific behavior

blocks.text: Adapter loading keeps the small LoRA adapter weights, covered in the earlier PEFT topic, as a separate artifact from the base model, applying them at inference time rather than baking them permanently into the model, this is the deployment-side counterpart to the training-side adapter workflow covered earlier in this course.
2. Merged vs Loaded Deployment

blocks.alt: A merged deployment bakes the adapter in while a loaded deployment keeps it separate

blocks.text: Merging an adapter into the base model, covered in the earlier PEFT topic merge_and_unload method, produces a standalone model with no runtime flexibility, keeping the adapter loaded separately trades a small amount of inference overhead for the ability to swap or combine adapters without redeploying the entire model.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Deployment Style","Tradeoff"],"rows":[["Merged","Simplest to serve, but fixed to one adapter permanently"],["Loaded","Slight runtime overhead, but flexible adapter swapping"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Serving Multiple Adapters From One Base Model

blocks.alt: A base model in memory serves adapter A, adapter B, and adapter C

blocks.text: Because adapter weights are small, covered in the earlier PEFT topic, a single base model kept in memory can serve many different loaded adapters simultaneously, each representing a different task or customer, avoiding the memory cost of hosting a fully separate model instance per task.

code.content:
from peft import PeftModel

base_model = load_base_model()
adapters = {
    "support": PeftModel.from_pretrained(base_model, "adapters/support"),
    "sales": PeftModel.from_pretrained(base_model, "adapters/sales"),
}
response = adapters[request.task].generate(request.prompt)

blocks.text: 4. Routing Requests to the Right Adapter

blocks.alt: An incoming request selects an adapter by task and routes to the loaded adapter

blocks.text: A serving system needs a routing layer that determines which loaded adapter should handle each incoming request, based on a task identifier, customer identifier, or similar signal, this routing decision determines which task-specific behavior the shared base model applies to that particular request.
5. Cold Loads vs Warm Loads

blocks.alt: A cold load with an uncached adapter is compared against a warm load with an already cached adapter

blocks.text: The first time a specific adapter is requested, a cold load, it needs to be read from storage and attached to the base model, adding latency, subsequent requests for the same adapter, a warm load, benefit from it already being resident in memory, caching frequently used adapters is a common optimization to minimize cold load latency.

blocks.title: Cold load latency is a real production concern
blocks.content: A system serving many rarely used adapters can see meaningfully worse tail latency from frequent cold loads, keeping the most frequently requested adapters warm, or pre-loading known high-traffic adapters, directly addresses this.

blocks.text: 6. The Cost of Swapping Adapters

blocks.alt: Swapping out adapter A and swapping in adapter B causes a brief latency spike

blocks.text: Even with adapters cached, actively swapping which adapter is attached to a shared model instance for consecutive requests carries some overhead, high-throughput serving systems often batch requests by adapter, covered further in the later Batch Inference topic, to minimize how often this swap actually needs to happen.
7. Memory Efficiency at Scale

blocks.alt: Shared base model memory supports many small loaded adapters

blocks.text: The core efficiency argument for adapter loading is memory, one copy of the base model in memory, potentially many gigabytes, can support dozens or hundreds of task-specific adapters, each only a few megabytes, a dramatically better memory profile than hosting a fully separate fine-tuned model per task.
8. When Merging Is Still the Right Choice

For a deployment that only ever needs one fixed adapter behavior, with no need to swap or support multiple tasks from the same instance, merging, covered in the earlier PEFT topic, remains simpler and avoids any runtime adapter-loading overhead entirely, the choice between merging and loading depends on whether runtime flexibility is actually needed.
9. Adapter Loading in Multi-Tenant Systems

Adapter loading is particularly well suited to multi-tenant systems, where each customer or use case has its own fine-tuned adapter, serving all of them from one shared base model instance rather than provisioning separate infrastructure per tenant meaningfully reduces infrastructure cost at scale.
Worked Example

A company serving fine-tuned assistants for many different enterprise customers keeps one shared base model in memory and loads each customer specific LoRA adapter, covered in earlier modules, on demand as requests arrive, rather than hosting a separate full model per customer.

They notice their least active customers experience noticeably higher first-request latency due to cold loads, so they add a warm cache that keeps the most recently and frequently used adapters resident in memory, reducing this latency for the vast majority of traffic while still supporting a long tail of less active customer adapters without provisioning dedicated infrastructure for each.
Common Mistakes

items: Merging an adapter into the base model when the actual deployment needs to support multiple swappable task behaviors
Not caching frequently used adapters, causing avoidable cold load latency on every request
Ignoring the routing logic needed to correctly direct each request to its matching loaded adapter
Overestimating memory savings by not accounting for the base model itself still needing to be resident in memory

blocks.text: Practice

For a multi-tenant fine-tuning deployment you are designing, decide whether merged or loaded adapter deployment fits better, and if loaded, sketch what caching strategy you would use to minimize cold load latency for your most frequently used adapters.
Key Takeaway

Adapter loading keeps LoRA adapters separate from the base model at deployment time, letting one shared base model instance serve many task-specific behaviors through dynamic runtime loading, trading a small overhead and cold-load latency consideration for major memory efficiency compared to merging or hosting separate models per task, especially valuable in multi-tenant serving systems.
